text: Raw pyodbc works fine, but pandas' to_sql method -- writing a whole DataFrame to a table in one call -- needs something pyodbc alone doesn't give you. That something is SQLAlchemy.

SQLAlchemy doesn't replace pyodbc -- it still uses pyodbc underneath for the actual SQL Server connection. What it adds is a consistent interface that pandas and other tools expect, instead of one driver-specific connection string.

Building an engine looks a lot like Lesson 26's connection string -- the same driver, server, database, and Windows authentication pieces -- just arranged as a URL. And create_engine doesn't connect right away; it builds a reusable object that opens connections as needed.
pd.read_sql works exactly the same as before, except now you pass it the engine instead of a raw connection. In practice, the engine version is what you'll see in most real pipeline code.

Here's the payoff: to_sql writes an entire DataFrame to a table in one call. It's doing what Lesson 28's executemany loop did by hand, except append adds rows to an existing table, replace drops and recreates it, and fail -- the default -- raises an error if the table's already there.

So when do you reach for which? Raw pyodbc is simpler for a one-off script where you want direct control over cursors and transactions. SQLAlchemy earns its setup once you're using to_sql regularly, or working across more than one database engine.
Next lesson ties the last piece together: what a transaction actually is, how rollback undoes a failed write, and a safe try, except, finally pattern you'll reuse for the rest of this course.
